hero.caption: A circular patch of trees remains in a field at 35°29′37.12″N 77°51′30.57″W in eastern North Carolina. This land is not plowed due to an easement the government took on the land around where a nuclear bomb landed during the 1961 Goldsboro B-52 crash. The nuclear bomb was only partially recovered and the secondary portion of it remains underneath this piece of land.

images.caption: Diagram of the external features of a Mark 39 nuclear bomb. The Access Panel to the Armed/Safe Switch is indicated. Section A contains the warhead. Section B contains the parachute pack. The text on the front of the bomb, per museum casings, likely said: "REJECT IF DENTED OR DEFORMED."

images.caption:
Weapon No. 1, a Mark 39 Mod 2 thermonuclear weapon, as found by the explosive ordnance disposal team after the Goldsboro accident in 1961. The text indicates where the "pull valve rod" and the "pull-out rods" were extracted, which began the firing sequence of the weapon. 
Note that another version of this image exists. That image, however, was photographically edited to be wider (probably for a television screen) using the "clone" tool on the left and right edges of it. This appears to be the correct dimensions of the original image.
images.alt:
Weapon No. 1, a Mark 39 Mod 2 thermonuclear weapon, as found by the explosive ordnance disposal team after the Goldsboro accident in 1961. The text indicates where the "pull valve rod" and the "pull-out rods" were extracted, which began the firing sequence of the weapon.

images.caption: The Mk 39 Mod 2 nuclear bomb designated as Weapon No. 1 in the 1961 Goldsboro B-52 accident, as it was discovered by EOD teams. The photograph is from a different angle than  File:Goldsboro Bomb Weapon 1 (LA-UR-20-22180).jpg this other one. The color is probably hand-tinting to a grayscale photograph (as the original scan shows considerable signs of color shift due to aging photopaper, which has been removed here, and the colors are "flat" and not exact in the ways of older methods). All Mk 39 casings in museums depict it as being a drab olive green. The original image carried the caption "FIN AND BODY DAMAGE" underneath it, along with the number B0332.
